comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
The surface question is settled on a_26BJb2n6o: seven verbs, shaped to
intents, and addressing via a `MUSTER_PANE` that Muster sets itself when
it creates the pane. That last part was the piece with no known answer -
herdr turns out to accept a per-pane `env` map on `pane.split`,
`tab.create` and `workspace.create` at the pinned version, so the CLI
never has to read a `HERDR_*` variable to know where it is.

Consequence for sequencing: a_294rihJCP owns that mechanism, so it lands
first, then a_26BJb2n6o, then this card is the scenario that proves both.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
The scenario, in the words it arrived in: spin up one agent, hand it a
list of cards and a workflow skill, and have it lay out the work - "you
are the integrator, split two panes below you, start an agent in each,
and give them their first instructions."

**The surface for this is Muster's own CLI (a_26BJb2n6o), not herdr's.**
That is worth stating first because the obvious shortcut is to let agents
shell out to `herdr`, and it is a shortcut that cannot be taken back.

Why not herdr, in the order the reasons actually bite:

1. **It cannot express the scenario across two machines.** A window can
   hold a local daemon beside a devenv over SSH. `herdr` inside a pane
   reaches *that pane's* daemon and nothing else, so an integrator cannot
   put an implementor on the devenv, and cannot ask what the window is
   showing, because no single daemon knows. Muster is the only thing that
   knows the window spans two.
2. **It silently does half of anything with a view consequence.** A split
   made behind Muster's back appears - view = f(daemon state) catches it -
   but nothing focuses it, zooms it, or decides which region shows it.
   Muster's keyboard cursor is view-local by design ("cursors are
   written, not read"), so the agent has no way to say where it wants to
   end up. The herdr route works for exactly the operations whose whole
   effect is daemon state, and quietly truncates the rest.
3. **It would make herdr unswappable.** "We never let one own our
   contract" - but a documented herdr-shaped agent surface is the
   contract, whatever the seam says, because every skill and script
   written against it becomes the thing a replacement has to provide.
   Right now nothing depends on it. That is what makes this cheap to
   decide today and expensive in a year.
4. **It leaks a vocabulary Muster already translates away.** Workspaces,
   right-and-down-only splits, tab labels that are bare numbers. The seam
   exists to spare people those, and an agent surface made of them hands
   them back.

**What the backend half being free actually buys us**, verified against
the pinned herdr rather than assumed: the CLI is mostly a thin front over
things that already work. From inside a pane, `$HERDR_PANE_ID` names it,
`pane split --direction down` makes the panes, `pane rename` takes emoji
and sticks, `pane run` briefs them, and all four came back correct. So
this is an ergonomics and vocabulary problem, not a capability one - the
expensive part is only the view ops, which is the part only Muster can do
anyway.

**Ergonomic to what we intend to support, not one verb per herdr verb.**
The clearest evidence is that the hand-driven version needed `sleep`
between making a pane and typing into it: a pane's program is spawned
when the pane is created, so text sent before the shell has drawn a
prompt races its first output. The suite already carries a comment about
that hazard, having been bitten by it. Every agent scripting this by hand
would have to rediscover that wait and would get it wrong under load. One
intent, one call - "make a pane below me, in this directory, running
this" - moves the race out of everybody's script and into one place that
gets it right. Spelling to design against rather than a proposal, but
roughly:

    muster pane new --below --cwd <dir> --run "claude" --name "🤖 A"
    muster window --json          # what is on screen, and where focus is
    muster focus <pane>

Two things fall out that are worth keeping:

- **An agent spawning agents gets clean children by construction.** A new
  pane is the daemon's child, so it inherits the daemon's allowlisted
  environment rather than the spawning agent's - no `CLAUDE_CODE_*`
  leaking a session token or turning transcripts off in the pane it just
  made. a_28YgGqYq7 bought that; this is the case that shows what for.
- **Naming is the obvious first use of a_2936QHMRa**, and one call. An
  integrator that names its implementors makes the sidebar readable at a
  glance.

**An agent has no eyes.** A person driving the GUI sees which panes are
on screen and where focus is; an agent has to ask. The reads matter at
least as much as the writes, and a CLI that only writes leaves an agent
arranging a window it cannot look at.

**Addressing, which is also discoverability.** A pane knows
`$HERDR_PANE_ID`, so an agent can tell it is inside herdr; nothing tells
it that it is inside Muster or that a view surface exists. A `MUSTER_*`
variable carried into panes solves both at once - it announces the
surface, and it says *which window* this pane belongs to, so `muster`
needs no `--window` flag in the common case. Worth designing with the CLI
rather than after it, because the CLI has to reach a running GUI process
somehow and this is the half that names the target.

Not blocked, and not pretended away: herdr sets `HERDR_*` in every pane
and Muster cannot hide that. The honest position is to say once, where
the seam is explained, that it is not the interface and will not track
Muster's vocabulary - agents will find it either way, and it is better
they know it is unsupported than assume it is the API.

Open question, deliberately left: **is the recipe a Muster feature or a
skill?** Lean: a skill. Muster's job is to make the surface drivable and
discoverable; it should not know what parallel-pr is, any more than it
knows what Claude Code is. The non-goal says so already - "Muster imposes
no workflow".
title: 🤝 An agent in a pane, driving the window it lives in
